q: If CO2 is unavailable, why do the light-dependent reactions eventually slow down, even in bright light?
options: CO2 is needed by photosystem II as the raw material to split water and release O2
Without CO2, chlorophyll molecules can no longer absorb light energy in the antenna
ATP and NADPH aren't used, so NADP+ and ADP run out and electron flow backs up
CO2 is the source of the protons that are pumped into the thylakoid lumen by the ETC
explanation: The thylakoid reactions need oxidised NADP+ to accept electrons from PSI and ADP + Pi for ATP synthase. When the Calvin cycle stops, these aren't regenerated: NADPH and ATP accumulate, electron flow stalls and O2 release falls. Excess absorbed energy can then damage the photosystems (photoinhibition) – one reason carotenoids and cyclic flow are protective.
